fit for embarkation." two corrections here. this page previously said 30 men , from a secondary account; the catalogue's transcription of the journal itself says 39 , and the coincidence with the a thing that is family tradition says that too, and is kept anyway, because pretending otherwise is how family myths become family history. the five labels documented a named source with a reference, and where possible the scan itself. inferred a reasoned conclusion drawn from documented facts, with the reasoning written out in full so that it can be overturned by anyone who finds it wanting. superseded asserted in the family record, and now displaced by a document that says otherwise. disputed asserted in the family record but unsupported, or contradicted, by what can be seen. family lore told, remembered, not corroborated. kept because it is precious; labelled because pretending otherwise is how family myths become family history. living people living people are omitted from this build entirely — not hidden, not gated behind a login, not present in the output at all. the rule is applied once, in code, at the boundary between the research data and the published site — so a person cannot be living on one page and dead on another. judging people only by their own dates does not work on a tree this size, because thousands of them have no dates at all: medieval nobility, unnamed spouses, half-remembered great-aunts. treating all of those as living is safe but useless — it would withhold the fourteenth century. so instead the build computes, for every person, an upper bound on their birth year : the latest year they could possibly have been born, given their own recorded events, their children's births, their marriages and their parents' bounds. somebody is published only when even that latest possible birth is more than a hundred years ago. every step of that reasoning is a genuine bound rather than a guess — a parent is at least fourteen years older than their child and at most sixty; a person existed at their own recorded events. a recorded birth is never overridden by inference, because an inference that made a living person look older would publish them. where nothing whatever is known, the person is presumed living. on this build the rule judges 2,034 of the 15,643 people in the tree to be living, and removes 4 from the ancestor set. where a living person sits between two published generations, the line is shown as continuing but the person is not named — and a living spouse, parent or child is not named on anybody else's page either. a removal request is honoured within days , without argument and without requiring a reason. where the data comes from, and what that means the spine of this archive is a myheritage family tree of 15,643 people, exported to gedcom and parsed here. that is a starting point and not an authority. an online tree records what somebody believed; south wales in 1832, shot a bushranger dead in the blue mountains in 1839, and finished as governor of brisbane gaol. he is the best-documented man in this archive, and until now nobody had written him down. when the archive stripped the sneyds of their invented descent from keele hall, it was braced to lose something. it gained this instead: not a squire but a sergeant of mounted police , and a life that can be traced through the birthplaces of his own children. how the keele descent was broken → hanley to sydney the 4th (king's own) born at hanley, stoke-on-trent, on 15 march 1810 and christened there on 28 april 1811, the son of samuel sneyd, a grocer of hanley , and elizabeth margaret oliver. in 1832 he came to new south wales with the 4th (king's own) regiment of foot — one of the regiments doing convict-guard duty in the colony, the same work that had brought major george pitt d'arcy out six years earlier. the other soldier in this family → on 13 february 1837 he married catherine margaret mulcahy at camden . their first child, william hartley sneyd — this archive's direct ancestor — was born at kempsey the following year. the army record private 1463, 80th foot, mounted police attached he is in the muster, and it complicates the obituary in an interesting way. name samuel sneyd year 1841 rank private service number 1463 unit 80th foot sub unit mounted police attached location parramatta, n.s.w. reference tna wo 12/8483 · british army, worldwide index 1841 two apparent contradictions, both of which resolve. the regiment. the obituary says the 4th (king's own) ; the 1841 muster says the 80th foot . both are likely true in sequence. the 4th left the colony in the later 1830s and the 80th replaced it — and a soldier who had just married locally, as he did at camden in february 1837, would volunteer into the incoming regiment rather than sail home. the 80th were the staffordshire volunteers , which for a hanley man is not a bad place to land. the rank. the press calls him serjeant sneyd in 1839; the muster calls him a private in 1841. that is not a demotion. the new south wales mounted police was staffed by detachments seconded from line regiments, and a man held police rank while remaining on his regiment's books at his regimental rank. he was a sergeant of police and a private of the 80th at the same time. checked and excluded. the organ two years after stepping off the ship, he put an organ into a brisbane church. the organ historical trust of australia records it: the first organ at all saints' was installed in the old church and used for the first time on wednesday 3 august 1864 . it was built by thomas jennings of london , and installed by mr paul atkinson , who appears to have been the organist of the church at this time. all saints' wickham terrace is the oldest church in the brisbane cbd. an instrument shipped from london, assembled by a man who had been an organist at bandon in county cork eleven years earlier, and played by him in a colonial town of a few thousand people. this is the one thing in the archive that is neither a date nor a document but a skill — something a man knew how to do, carried nine thousand miles, and used. it is also, incidentally, an independent confirmation that the family reached brisbane by 1864. the limerick problem his wife jane creech was also of limerick, born the name d'arcy was coined twice over — once in normandy as the name of a place, once in ireland as the name of a colour. anyone searching the name needs to know that before they start. there is no single founding d'arcy family . the name reaches the english-speaking world by two entirely independent routes, and this is a method problem before it is a history. norman — the name of a place d'arcy is french for "of arcy" : a man named for the land he held. the place is usually given as arcy in la manche, normandy ; some accounts point instead to bois-d'arcy in the yvelines, west of paris. a norman de areci appears as a tenant-in-chief in lincolnshire in the reign of william i. by this route the name is territorial . it tells you where a family held land, and nothing whatever about what they were like. gaelic — the name of a colour darcy , characteristically without the apostrophe, is an anglicisation of o dorchaidhe , from dorcha , "dark" — dark-haired, dark-complexioned, or figuratively secretive. it is a nickname name, and there is nothing norman about it at all. the apostrophe is a hint and not a proof. it leans norman, and it was added, dropped and re-added by clerks, priests, recruiting sergeants and shipping agents for four hundred years. our own family is written both ways across its own records — and its most distinctive given name, lindesay , is spelled lindsay in the very next generation. see the spine → the most misused fact in d'arcy genealogy the tribes of galway the seventeenth-century genealogist dubhaltach macfhirbhisigh records that walter riabhach o dorchaidhe (fl. c. 1488) was "the first man of the ui dorchaidhe who came to galway, according to the galweigians themselves". his descendants became d'arcy , and d'arcy is counted among the tribes of galway , the fourteen merchant families who ran that city. this matters because of how it is habitually used. the galway d'arcys are gaelic o dorchaidhe who adopted a norman-looking spelling . they are not the norman de arcy of lincolnshire. a pedigree that climbs to "the d'arcys of galway" and then steps across to normandy has crossed between two unrelated families at exactly the point where the record is thinnest — and it is a step people take constantly, because it makes the better story. distribution forebears, spelling darcy , accessed 9 september 2026: 17,796 bearers
